mainTopic: Whether a master may tell his slave 'Work for me, and I will not feed you,' after setting aside the proof from the פאה dispute
overview: The amud opens by knocking down a proof. The גמרא had tried to settle whether someone who grabs property for a creditor acquires it, by linking it to the dispute between רבי אליעזר and the רבנן about gathering פאה for a poor friend. The גמרא shows that each side may rely on its own special reason: a מיגו for רבי אליעזר, and a פסוק for the רבנן. It then explains how רבי אליעזר reads that פסוק. Next, the גמרא infers from the משנה that a master may tell his slave, 'Work for me, and I will not feed you.' It pushes this aside by saying the master may have let the slave keep his earnings for his food. The same answer is defended against a ברייתא about a slave and a wife exiled to the ערי מקלט, and against a dispute between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and חכמים about a slave in years of famine. Finally the גמרא brings a proof from רב about a slave whose work was given to the הקדש. It rejects that proof too, and its challenge to that rejection continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר's view may rest on a special reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. רבי אליעזר may allow gathering פאה for a friend only because of a מיגו: the gatherer could have become poor himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps that is not so. רבי אליעזר only said it there because the gatherer could make all his property ownerless, become poor, and then be allowed to take the פאה himself. Since he could acquire it for himself, he can acquire it for his friend. But here, with the creditor, no such reasoning applies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof it just gave. It says the פאה dispute may have nothing to do with grabbing property for a creditor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר's ruling may depend on a special מיגו: the gatherer could have taken the פאה for himself, so he can also take it for someone else. A person grabbing for a creditor has no such power, since he could never grab that property for himself. So רבי אליעזר might agree that the grabber does not acquire.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps it is not so (a formula that rejects a proof)
He only said his ruling there (limiting a ruling to its own case)
Since; the logic that since he could do X, he can also do Y

phrases.english: Perhaps it is not so;

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר הָתָם,
phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer only said his ruling there
phrases.notes: "There" means the case of someone who gathered פאה and said it was for a poor friend.

phrases.english: because, since if he wanted,
he could make his property ownerless,
and become a poor man, and it would be fit for him;
and since he can acquire it for himself,
he can acquire it for his fellow;
but here, no.
phrases.notes: "Here" means grabbing property for a creditor, which the grabber could never take for himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought just before this section, which linked the creditor question to the פאה dispute.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that רבי אליעזר's view in the פאה case proves that grabbing for a creditor works.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי אליעזר's view may rest on a מיגו (he could have become poor and taken it himself), and this does not exist in the creditor case.

steps.title: The רבנן's view may rest on a verse
steps.stepSummary: The rejection continues from the other side. The רבנן may forbid gathering for a poor person only because of a פסוק, which does not apply to creditors.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן only said it there because it is written, 'Do not gather for the poor,' meaning you may not gather on behalf of a poor person. But here, with the creditor, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the rejection by showing that the רבנן's view also may not prove anything about creditors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן may agree that, in general, a person can acquire for someone else even when it hurts others. They forbid it in the פאה case only because the פסוק is read as one phrase: 'do not gather for the poor.' Since each side has its own special reason, the פאה dispute tells us nothing about the creditor question.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (introduces a פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: The פאה dispute cannot settle the creditor question. רבי אליעזר may rely on a מיגו, and the רבנן may rely on a פסוק, and neither reason applies to grabbing for a creditor.

phrases.aramaic: וְעַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמְרִי רַבָּנַן הָתָם,
phrases.english: And the Rabbis only said their ruling there
because it is written:
"You shall not gather... for the poor"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 23:22. In the פסוק these words are in two separate phrases; here they are read together.

phrases.english: meaning, you shall not gather for him, for the poor person;
but here, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמְרִי רַבָּנַן הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second half of the same rejection. Step 1 dealt with רבי אליעזר; this step deals with the רבנן.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the רבנן's view in the פאה case proves that grabbing for a creditor fails.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The רבנן's ruling may come from a special reading of a פסוק that applies only to gathering for the poor.

steps.title: How does רבי אליעזר read the verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי אליעזר does with the פסוק 'do not gather for the poor,' since he does not forbid gathering for a poor person.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אליעזר, what does he do with this phrase 'you shall not gather'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a side question about רבי אליעזר. It is setting up the answer that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 said the רבנן learn from this פסוק that one may not gather for a poor person. רבי אליעזר disagrees with that ruling. So the גמרא wants to know what he learns from these words instead.

keyTerms.meaning: What does he do with it? (How does he use this פסוק?)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Eliezer,
this phrase "you shall not gather",
what does he do with it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר, הַאי לֹא תְלַקֵּט מַאי עָבֵיד לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the פסוק raised in step 2 and asks how the other side uses it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What רבי אליעזר learns from the words 'לא תלקט'.

steps.title: The verse warns a poor man about his own field
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר uses the פסוק to teach that a poor man may not take פאה from his own field.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs it to warn a poor man about his own field: even though he is poor, he may not gather פאה from it for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. רבי אליעזר learns a different law from this פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר does not read the פסוק as 'do not gather for the poor.' He reads it as a warning to the field owner, even a poor one, not to gather the פאה of his own field. So the פסוק is still used, just for a different law.

keyTerms.meaning: To warn (to make it a prohibition)

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides use the פסוק 'לא תלקט.' The רבנן learn that one may not gather for a poor person. רבי אליעזר learns that a poor owner may not take פאה from his own field.

phrases.english: He needs it
to warn a poor man regarding his own field.
phrases.notes: Even a poor man who owns a field may not take its פאה for himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְהַזְהִיר לְעָנִי עַל שֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אליעזר uses the פסוק to forbid a poor field owner from taking the פאה of his own field.

steps.title: Inferring that a master may refuse to feed his working slave
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה, 'if he wishes not to feed him,' and concludes that a master may tell his slave, 'Work for me, but I will not feed you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'For if he wishes not to feed his slave, he may do so.' Learn from this that a master can say to his slave: 'Work for me, and I will not feed you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new line of the משנה and draws a conclusion from it. This conclusion will be discussed in what follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says a master is allowed not to feed his slave. The גמרא takes this to mean the master has no duty to feed him at all, even while the slave keeps working for him. This is a strong conclusion, and the גמרא will go on to test it.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it (a conclusion drawn from a source)

steps.whyThisMatters: This proposed inference opens a long search for a source that proves whether a master may make his slave work without feeding him. Each proof brought on this amud is pushed aside, and the last answer is being challenged as the amud ends.

phrases.english: The משנה said: "For if he wishes not to feed," etc.
Learn from this
that the master can say to the slave:
"Work for me, and I will not feed you"?

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁמְעַתְּ מִינַּהּ, יָכוֹל הָרַב לוֹמַר לָעֶבֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic based on the משנה, separate from the creditor and פאה discussion.
steps.raayaObject: That a master may make his slave work without feeding him.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's words 'שאם ירצה שלא לזון... רשאי.'

steps.title: The master let the slave keep his own earnings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from the משנה. The master did not keep the slave's work for nothing. He told the slave to use his own earnings to feed himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the master told the slave: 'Go, and use what you earn for your own food.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from Step 5. It says the משנה is talking about a master who let the slave keep his own earnings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 read the משנה as saying a master can take the slave's work and still not feed him. The גמרא answers that the משנה can be read as a fair trade: the master gives up the slave's earnings, and the slave feeds himself. So the משנה does not prove that a master can take work without giving food.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
Go (here meaning: go and manage on your own)
Your earnings, literally 'the work of your hands'

steps.confusionAlert: The master is not saying 'Work for me and I won't feed you.' He is saying 'Don't work for me. Keep your earnings and feed yourself.' Those are two very different deals.

phrases.english: With what case are we dealing here?
Where he said to him: 'Go, use your earnings for your food.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 5 by narrowing the case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the משנה line 'if he wishes not to feed him.'
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה may be talking about a master who gave the slave his earnings in exchange for not feeding him.

steps.title: Then why can't a husband make the same deal with his wife?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer. If the same deal works for a slave, it should also work for a wife. Yet the source treats the wife differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then in the matching case of a wife, it should also mean he told her: 'Go, use your earnings for your food.' Why can't he do that with a wife?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks Step 6. It points to the matching ruling about a wife in the same source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source separates a slave from a wife: a husband cannot stop feeding his wife. But a husband is allowed to let his wife keep her earnings in exchange for her food. If the slave case is only about that kind of trade, the wife case should allow it too. So why does the source treat them differently?

phrases.english: The matching case regarding a wife
would be where he said to her: 'Go, use your earnings for your food'?!
With a wife, why can't he?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading in Step 6, that the master told the slave to use his own earnings for food.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that reading were right, the matching wife case would also be allowed. But the source treats the wife differently.

steps.title: The wife's earnings are not enough to feed her
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the wife in the source cannot support herself. In that case the husband may not make the deal.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wife in that case is one whose earnings are not enough to feed her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 7 by describing the wife's situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A husband may let his wife keep her earnings for her food only if those earnings are enough to feed her. The source is talking about a wife who earns too little, so the husband must still feed her. That explains why she is treated differently from the slave.

keyTerms.meaning: It is enough (her earnings cover her needs)

phrases.english: A wife, where [her earnings] are not enough.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from Step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case limitation: the wife's case involves earnings that are too small.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The wife case and the slave case are the same deal, so they should get the same ruling.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wife cannot live on her earnings, so the husband must still feed her.

steps.title: Then say the slave also cannot support himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back. Read the slave case the same way, as a slave who cannot support himself. Then the master could still refuse to feed him, and the original proof comes back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then say the slave also has earnings that are not enough!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer in Step 8 by applying the same idea to the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the wife case is about earnings that are too small, the slave case should be about the same thing. That would mean the master may refuse to feed a slave who cannot support himself. If so, the earlier proof works again: a master can avoid feeding his slave.

keyTerms.meaning: It is enough (same word as for the wife, used for the slave)

phrases.english: The slave too, where [his earnings] are not enough!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 8 by reading the slave case the same way.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in Step 8 that separates the wife from the slave.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two cases sit side by side in the source, so they should be read the same way. That would bring back the proof that a master can refuse to feed his slave.

steps.title: A slave not worth his food is useless to his owner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that nobody keeps a slave who cannot even earn his own food. So the slave case must be about a slave who can support himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: A slave who is not even worth the bread he eats, what would his master or mistress want him for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge in Step 9. It explains why the slave case cannot be about a slave who earns too little.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slave is kept for his work. A slave whose work does not even cover his food is of no use, so the source would not be talking about him. A marriage, though, does not depend on how much the wife earns. So the two cases really are different, and the proof from the משנה stays rejected.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה cannot prove that a master may say 'Work for me, and I won't feed you.' It may be talking about a slave who keeps his own earnings and can live on them.

phrases.english: A slave who is not worth the bread of his belly,
what would his master or his mistress need him for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 9 and keeps the rejection from Step 6 in place.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reasoning: the slave case cannot be about a slave who earns too little.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The slave case could be about a slave who cannot support himself.
steps.terutzMaskana: Nobody keeps such a slave, so the case is about a slave who can feed himself from his earnings.

steps.title: New proof from a slave exiled to a city of refuge
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a slave exiled to the ערי מקלט. His master does not have to feed him, yet the master still gets his earnings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a slave who was exiled to a city of refuge does not have to be fed by his master. Not only that, his earnings go to his master. Learn from this that a master can tell his slave: 'Work for me, and I won't feed you!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new proof for the same question, this time from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case the master gets the slave's earnings but does not feed him. That looks like exactly the deal being asked about: work without food. So the גמרא suggests the master is allowed to make it.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (brings a source as proof)
Cities of refuge, for someone who killed by accident

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע: עֶבֶד שֶׁגָּלָה לְעָרֵי מִקְלָט
phrases.english: Come and hear: a slave who was exiled to a city of refuge,
his master is not obligated to feed him,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא עוֹד אֶלָּא שֶׁמַּעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו לְרַבּוֹ.
phrases.english: and not only that, but his earnings belong to his master.
Learn from this
that a master can say to the slave:
'Work for me, and I won't feed you!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was rejected, the גמרא tries a new one.
steps.raayaObject: That a master may say to his slave, 'Work for me, and I won't feed you.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: a slave exiled to a city of refuge is not fed by his master, yet his earnings go to the master.

steps.title: Here too, the master gave the slave his earnings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the new proof the same way as before. The case is one where the master told the slave to use his earnings for his food.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the master told him: 'Go, use your earnings for your food.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the city-of-refuge proof with the same answer it gave in Step 6.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא can be read as talking about a master who told the slave to feed himself from his earnings. Read this way, the master never took the slave's work without giving him food, so the proof falls away. The next step asks how this fits with the ברייתא's words that the earnings go to the master.
steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs are rejected the same way: 'צֵא מַעֲשֵׂה יָדֶיךָ לִמְזוֹנוֹתֶיךָ'. The slave feeds himself from his own earnings. So we still have no proof that a master may say 'Work for me, and I won't feed you.'

phrases.english: With what case are we dealing here?
Where he said to him: 'Go, use your earnings for your food.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 11 the same way Step 6 rejected the first proof.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the city-of-refuge ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא may be talking about a master who let the slave feed himself from his earnings, so no work was taken without food.

steps.title: If the master said so, why does he get the slave's earnings?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 12. If the master told the slave to feed himself from his earnings, how can the ברייתא say the earnings belong to the master?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do his earnings belong to his master?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pokes a hole in the answer it just gave in step 12.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 said the master told the slave to use his earnings for his food. But the ברייתא says the master gets the slave's מעשה ידיו. If the earnings go toward the slave's food, how can they also go to the master?

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if what you just said is true)
His earnings (literally, the work of his hands)

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: Meaning: if the master really told the slave to feed himself from his earnings, as step 12 said.

phrases.english: why do his earnings go to his master?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, מַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו אַמַּאי לְרַבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the case setup proposed in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The step 12 answer that the master told the slave to use his earnings for food.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under that setup, the earnings feed the slave. That seems to clash with the ברייתא's ruling that the earnings belong to the master.

steps.title: The master gets only the leftover earnings
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא means the master gets the העדפה, whatever the slave earns beyond what he needs for food.
steps.simpleTranslation: It means the surplus.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the master does not get all the earnings, only what is left over after the slave's food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slave uses his earnings to feed himself, as the master told him. Anything extra still belongs to the master, because the slave is his. So both parts of the ברייתא now fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: Surplus, the earnings left over after paying for food

phrases.english: For the surplus.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing what the ruling refers to
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'His earnings go to his master' means all of his earnings.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means only the leftover earnings beyond the slave's food.

steps.title: Isn't it obvious that the surplus goes to the master?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needed to teach something so obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: The surplus? That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer by saying the ברייתא would then be teaching something everyone already knows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The master owns the slave, so of course extra earnings go to him. A ברייתא should not need to say something that plain.

phrases.english: The surplus? That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תירוץ of step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא is talking about the העדפה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that is all it means, the ruling is too obvious to need saying.

steps.title: You might have thought the master loses the surplus too
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is needed. You might have thought that since the master gives nothing when the slave earns too little, he also takes nothing when the slave earns extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: since when the slave doesn't have enough, the master doesn't give him anything, then when he has extra, the master also shouldn't take it from him. So the ברייתא teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the ruling about the surplus is not obvious after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There seems to be a fairness argument. If the master won't cover a shortfall, maybe he also shouldn't get the extra. The ברייתא teaches that the master still gets the surplus anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken assumption)
It teaches us (that the assumption is wrong)

phrases.english: You might have said,

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דְּכִי לֵית לֵיהּ לָא יָהֵיב לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: since when he doesn't have, he doesn't give him,
phrases.notes: He means: when the slave doesn't earn enough for food, the master doesn't make up the difference.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אִית לֵיהּ נָמֵי לָא לִישְׁקוֹל מִינֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: then when he has extra, he also should not take it from him,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא, כֵּיוָן דְּכִי לֵית לֵיהּ לָא יָהֵיב לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the ruling was needed to block a mistaken assumption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because the master won't cover a shortfall, he also shouldn't keep the surplus.
steps.terutzMaskana: The surplus still belongs to the master.

steps.title: Why mention the ערי מקלט at all?
steps.stepSummary: If the surplus rule applies to every slave, why does the ברייתא state it about a slave exiled to the ערי מקלט?
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is different about the ערי מקלט?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא chose to state this rule specifically about an exiled slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to steps 14 to 16, the surplus goes to the master wherever the slave lives. So mentioning the ערי מקלט seems to add nothing. The גמרא wants to know what that detail is there for.

keyTerms.meaning: Cities of refuge, where someone who killed by accident is exiled

phrases.english: And what is different about the cities of refuge?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues testing the reading of the ברייתא built in steps 12 to 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's mention of ערי מקלט, under the current reading.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the rule applies to every slave, the detail about the ערי מקלט looks unnecessary.

steps.title: "And live": you might have given the exile extra
steps.stepSummary: Because of the פסוק 'וָחָי', you might have thought an exiled slave should get extra help to live, including keeping his surplus. The ברייתא teaches that this is not so.
steps.simpleTranslation: It might enter your mind to say: the פסוק says 'and he shall live', so we should give him extra means of living. So the ברייתא teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the ערי מקלט detail is there to block a special reason for letting the exiled slave keep his surplus.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה says the exile flees to a city of refuge 'and lives'. You might think this means we must make his life easier, so he keeps the extra he earns. The ברייתא teaches that even an exiled slave's surplus goes to his master.

keyTerms.meaning: It might enter your mind to say
And he shall live (from the פסוק about ערי מקלט)

phrases.english: It might enter your mind to say:
"And he shall live" —
we should give him extra means of living,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that a detail was needed to block a mistaken assumption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because of 'וָחָי', the exiled slave should keep his surplus.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even in the ערי מקלט, the surplus goes to the master.

steps.title: The exiled wife shows nothing was said
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא of the ברייתא says a husband must feed his exiled wife. That only makes sense if he never told her to use her earnings for food. So the ברייתא seems to be about a case where nothing was said, and that undermines the step 12 answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: But since the latter part of the ברייתא teaches: 'However, a woman who was exiled to the ערי מקלט, her husband must feed her,' this shows he did not tell her to use her earnings. For if he had told her, why would her husband have to feed her?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a strong challenge from the second half of the same ברייתא against the answer given in step 12.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the husband had told his wife to use her earnings for food, he would not have to feed her. Since the סיפא says he must, it is talking about a case where nothing was said. That suggests the רישא about the slave is also a case where nothing was said, which brings back the original proof.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter clause of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not attacking the law about the wife. It uses the wife clause to prove what kind of case the whole ברייתא is about: one where nothing was said. That knocks out the step 12 answer for the slave.
steps.whyThisMatters: If this challenge holds, the step 12 answer is gone, and the ברייתא again seems to prove that a master can stop feeding a slave without any agreement.

phrases.english: But since the latter clause teaches:
However, a woman who was exiled to the cities of refuge —
her husband must provide her food;
this shows that he did not tell her,
phrases.notes: Meaning: he never said to her, 'Use your earnings for your food.'

phrases.english: for if he had told her,
why would her husband be obligated?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא מִדְּקָתָנֵי סֵיפָא: אֲבָל אִשָּׁה שֶׁגָּלְתָה לְעָרֵי מִקְלָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to attack the step 12 answer, now using the סיפא of the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The step 12 answer that the ברייתא is about a master who told his slave to use his earnings for food.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא only makes sense where nothing was said. So the ברייתא as a whole is about such a case, and the slave clause again shows a master need not feed his slave.

steps.title: If the wife's case is where nothing was said, so is the slave's
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the challenge from step 19. Since the סיפא about the wife is a case where the husband said nothing, the רישא about the עבד must also be a case where the master said nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And since the second part (about the wife) is a case where he did not tell her, the first part (about the slave) must also be a case where he did not tell him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the attack it started in step 19. It argues that both halves of the ברייתא must be talking about the same kind of case: one where nothing was said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two halves of a ברייתא are normally read as matching cases. If the wife's half is a case where the husband said nothing, the עבד's half must be too. That breaks the earlier answer from step 12, which needed the עבד case to be one where the master did say 'use your earnings for your food.'

keyTerms.meaning: The later part of a משנה or ברייתא
The first part of a משנה or ברייתא

phrases.english: And since the latter clause is where he did not say to her,
phrases.notes: The latter clause is the wife's case. 'Say' means telling her to use her earnings for her food.

phrases.english: the first clause is also where he did not say to him!
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the עבד. The master never told him to support himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִדְּסֵיפָא דְּלָא אֲמַר לַהּ, רֵישָׁא נָמֵי דְּלָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge begun in step 19 by stating its conclusion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The step 12 answer, that the עבד case is one where the master said 'use your earnings for your food.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both halves of the ברייתא should describe the same kind of case. If the wife's half is where nothing was said, the עבד's half must be too.

steps.title: Both cases are where he spoke, but the wife's earnings fall short
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that both halves really are cases where he said 'use your earnings for your food.' The husband must still feed his wife because her earnings are not enough to cover her food.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is a case where he did say it to him. And the woman's case is where her earnings were not enough.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the step 12 answer. Both halves are cases where he said it. The wife still needs her husband's support because her earnings don't cover her food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband's duty to feed his wife does not prove he said nothing. Even after he says it, he must make up the difference if her earnings are too small. So both halves can match after all.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually. Used to keep the original reading

phrases.english: Actually, it is where he said to him,
and the woman is where it was not sufficient.
phrases.notes: Meaning her earnings were not enough to pay for her food, so the husband covers the rest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 19–20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case (אוקימתא): the wife's earnings fall short.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The husband feeding his wife means he never told her to support herself.
steps.terutzMaskana: He did tell her, but her earnings were not enough, so he must make up the difference.

steps.title: The next line implies the earlier line had no statement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again. The ברייתא goes on to say 'and if he told her to use her earnings for her food, he may.' That implies the line before it, where the husband must feed her, is a case where he did not tell her.
steps.simpleTranslation: But since the last part teaches, 'And if he said to her, use your earnings for your food, he is allowed,' this shows that the part before it is where he did not say it to her!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer of step 21 by reading the wording of the ברייתא closely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'and if he said to her' introduce a new case. That makes it sound like the line before it, 'he must feed her,' was a case where he said nothing. If so, step 21's reading is wrong.
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'רישא' does not mean the עבד case. It means the first line of the wife's section ('her husband must feed her'), before the line 'and if he said to her.'

phrases.english: But since the last clause teaches:
And if he said to her
'Use your earnings for your food,' he is permitted,
this implies that the first clause is where he did not say to her!
phrases.notes: The 'first clause' here is the line right before: the husband must feed his exiled wife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 21 using the wording of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 21's claim that the wife's case is one where he did say it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'And if he said to her' marks a new case. So the line before it must be where he did not say it.

steps.title: Reading the ending as: if her earnings are enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains what the ברייתא means: 'And if her earnings are enough, and he told her to use them for her food, he is allowed.'
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it is saying: And if her earnings are enough, and he said to her, 'Use your earnings for your food,' he is allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the wording problem by showing what the last line really adds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference between the two lines is not whether he spoke. In both he spoke. The difference is whether her earnings are enough. If they are not, he must make up the rest. If they are, he owes nothing more.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means to say
Her earnings are enough to cover her needs

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
And if her earnings are sufficient, and he said to her:
'Use your earnings for your food,' he is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the wording (הכי קאמר): the new condition is 'her earnings are enough,' not 'he spoke.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'And if he said to her' means the earlier line had no statement.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both lines involve a statement. The earlier line is where her earnings fall short, and the later line is where they are enough.

steps.title: Why say this about an exiled wife?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needs to teach this about an exiled wife whose earnings are enough. Any husband may tell such a wife to support herself.
steps.simpleTranslation: If her earnings are enough, why does it need to be said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions why this line about an exiled wife is needed at all. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every husband may tell a wife whose earnings are enough to support herself. So why teach it about a wife exiled to an עיר מקלט? This is the same kind of question the גמרא asked about the עבד in step 17.

keyTerms.meaning: Why does it need to be said? (It seems obvious)

phrases.english: If it is sufficient, what is the point of saying it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the need for the line as it was reread in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the ברייתא to teach this about an exiled wife.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This rule applies to all wives, so stating it about an exiled wife seems pointless.

steps.title: Because of 'כל כבודה בת מלך פנימה'
steps.stepSummary: The line is needed. Because of the פסוק 'כל כבודה בת מלך פנימה,' you might have thought an exiled wife in a strange city should not have to work. The ברייתא teaches that her husband may still tell her to support herself.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: 'All the honor of the king's daughter is inside' (so a woman in exile should not be sent out to work). It teaches us that he may still tell her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the line is not obvious, because a פסוק could have led us to a different rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק teaches that a woman's dignity is in staying home. So you might think a wife in an עיר מקלט should be spared from working. The ברייתא tells us there is no such special rule, and the usual rule applies. This matches step 18, where the exiled עבד also got no special treatment.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken idea)
'All the honor of the king's daughter is inside.' A woman's dignity is in staying home
It teaches us (that this is not so)

steps.whatToRemember: Both halves of the ברייתא are cases where he said 'use your earnings for your food.' If a wife's earnings are not enough, her husband makes up the rest. If they are enough, he owes nothing more. Being in exile changes nothing for the עבד or the wife.
steps.whyThisMatters: This saves the step 12 answer. The ברייתא is fully about cases where the statement was made, and both halves match.

phrases.english: Lest you say:
'All the honor of the king's daughter is within,'
it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: הוה אמינא (מהו דתימא): a פסוק might have suggested a special rule for an exiled wife.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because of 'כל כבודה בת מלך פנימה,' an exiled wife should not be made to work for her food.
steps.terutzMaskana: Her husband may still tell her to use her earnings for her food.

steps.title: Suggesting the question is an old dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that whether a master may stop feeding his slave is already argued by תנאים. It quotes a ברייתא where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and חכמים disagree about a slave in years of famine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this is a dispute between תנאים. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: In years of famine a slave can say to his master, 'Either feed me or set me free.' חכמים say: The master gets to decide.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to see if our question about feeding a slave was already argued by earlier sages. This sets up the next step, where the גמרא explains how the ברייתא would fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase לימא כתנאי means 'shall we say this is a dispute between תנאים?' רבן שמעון בן גמליאל lets the slave push his master, and חכמים leave the choice with the master. The גמרא hopes to match these two sides to the two sides of our question.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say this is a dispute between תנאים?
Years of famine, when food is scarce and expensive
The choice is in the master's hands

phrases.english: Let us say it is like a dispute of תנאים:
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
A slave can say to his master
in years of famine:
'Either feed me, or set me free.'
And the Sages say:
The choice is in his master's hands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the wife discussion (Steps 21-25) back to the slave question, and tries to find it in a dispute between תנאים.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a master may tell his slave to work for him without feeding him
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with a dispute between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and חכמים about a slave in years of famine

steps.title: Proposing what the two sides argue about
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that חכמים hold a master may stop feeding his slave, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds he may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this what they argue about? One sage holds the master can say 'work for me and I won't feed you,' and the other holds he cannot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out its suggested reading: the ברייתא is our exact question, with each sage taking one side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חכמים say the master decides, so they would hold he can stop feeding the slave. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the slave can demand food or freedom, so he would hold the master cannot. If this is right, our question is simply an old argument.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it that...? (opens a suggested reading)

phrases.english: What, don't they argue about this:
that one sage holds: he can,
phrases.notes: This is חכמים: the master can tell his slave to work without being fed.

phrases.english: and the other sage holds: he cannot?
phrases.notes: This is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the ברייתא quoted in Step 26 would match our question.
steps.raayaObject: That the question of feeding a slave is a dispute between תנאים
steps.raayaSupportSource: Reading רבן שמעון בן גמליאל as 'cannot' and חכמים as 'can'

steps.title: Two problems with that reading
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. If the argument were about the master stopping food, the slave should demand 'feed me or give me my earnings,' not 'free me.' Also, why mention years of famine at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: Do you really think so? This wording, 'feed me or set me free'? He should have said, 'feed me or give me my earnings for my food!' And also: what is special about years of famine?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggested reading with two problems.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Problem one: if the master just stopped feeding the slave, the fair demand would be to keep his own earnings, not to go free. Problem two: if the argument were about stopping food in general, it would apply in every year, so the famine detail makes no sense. Together these show the ברייתא is about something else.

keyTerms.meaning: Do you really think so? (introduces a rejection)
My earnings, what I produce with my work

phrases.english: Do you really think so?!
This, 'either feed me or set me free'?!
'Either feed me or give me
my earnings for my food' is what he should have said!
And also: what is different about years of famine?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reading offered in Step 27.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the ברייתא is about whether a master may stop feeding his slave
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The demand to be freed does not fit that case, and the famine detail would be pointless

steps.title: The real case: the master told him to live off his earnings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the ברייתא is about a master who told the slave to use his earnings for food. In famine years the earnings are not enough, and that is where the sages argue.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what case are we dealing with here? Where the master told him, 'Use your earnings for your food,' and in years of famine the earnings are not enough.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new reading of the ברייתא that solves both problems from the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees the master may tell the slave to live off his earnings, so this is no longer our question. The argument only starts in famine, when food costs more and his earnings cannot cover it. That explains why famine is mentioned and why the slave asks to be freed: he already has his earnings, and they are not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?
Use your earnings for your food

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא is not about whether a master may stop feeding his slave. It is about a slave already told to live off his earnings, when famine makes those earnings too small.
steps.confusionAlert: This is the same idea as the wife case in Steps 21-23: telling someone to live off their earnings is allowed, and the problem only comes up when the earnings are not enough.

phrases.english: Rather, what are we dealing with here?
Where he said to him, 'Use your earnings for your food,'
and in years of famine it is not enough;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new reading of the ברייתא that avoids both problems raised in Step 28.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא argues about whether a master may stop feeding his slave
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about a slave told to live off his earnings, which fall short in famine years

steps.title: Why each side argues about the slave in famine years
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the slave may demand 'feed me or free me' so that people will see him and give him charity. חכמים say people who give to the poor will give to a slave too, so he does not need to be freed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that the slave can say: 'Either feed me or set me free, so that people will see me and have mercy on me.' חכמים hold that whoever has mercy on free people will have mercy on a slave too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its new reading of the ברייתא by giving each side's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The master already told the slave to live off his own earnings, and in a famine those earnings are not enough. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל thinks a slave would not get charity, so freeing him is his only way to survive. חכמים think charity givers help slaves too, so there is no reason to free him. Because of this, the ברייתא proves nothing about whether a master may stop feeding his slave.

keyTerms.meaning: Have mercy, meaning people give charity

steps.whatToRemember: In this reading, the famine argument is only about whether a slave can get charity while still a slave. It is not about a master refusing to feed him, so the גמרא looks for another proof in the next step.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds:
Either feed me or set me free,
so that people will see me
and have mercy on me.
And the Rabbis hold:
Whoever has mercy on free people
will also have mercy on a slave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes step 29's new reading by giving each side's reasoning.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (the master told the slave to live off his earnings)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to be an argument about whether a master may stop feeding his slave.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is only about whether a slave who cannot get by on his earnings must be freed so that he can get charity.

steps.title: A proof from רב about a slave whose work was given to the Temple
steps.stepSummary: רב says that if a master makes his slave's work belong to the הקדש, the slave borrows money to eat and later works to pay it back. The גמרא concludes that a master may say 'work for me and I won't feed you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, for רב said: If someone makes his slave's hands holy, that slave borrows and eats, and then works and pays back. Learn from this that a master can say to his slave: 'Work for me, and I will not feed you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new proof, a statement of רב, to answer the question of whether a master may stop feeding his slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the slave's work goes to the הקדש, the master no longer gets anything from it, yet רב does not say the master must feed him. Instead, the slave has to borrow for his food. The גמרא reads this as proof that a master is not required to feed his slave.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, introducing a proof
One who makes his slave's work belong to the הקדש
Work for me, and I will not feed you

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Rav said:
One who consecrates the hands of his slave,
phrases.notes: "Hands" means his work. Everything he earns now belongs to the Temple.

phrases.english: that slave borrows and eats,
and works and pays back.
Learn from this:
the master is able to say to the slave:
"Work for me, and I will not feed you"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The proof from the ברייתא failed, so the גמרא tries a new source.
steps.raayaObject: That a master may say 'work for me and I won't feed you.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב: when a slave's work belongs to the הקדש, the slave borrows to eat. The master is not made to feed him.

steps.title: רב's case is where the master does feed him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב is talking about a master who does give his slave food, so there is no proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? One where the master gives the slave his food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by saying רב's case is one where the master is already feeding the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the master really does feed him, רב's ruling says nothing about whether a master may refuse to feed his slave. The proof falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? Used to narrow a source to a specific case

phrases.english: Here, what are we dealing with?
Where he provides him with food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from רב in step 31.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof completely by limiting רב's statement to a narrow case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the master was not feeding the slave. But רב may be talking about a master who does feed him.

steps.title: If the master feeds him, why would he need to borrow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to challenge the answer: if the master gives food, why does the slave need to borrow?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, for what...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move: a challenge to the answer it just gave. The rest of the question continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the master really feeds the slave, then the words 'borrows and eats' in רב's statement seem to have no purpose. The גמרא is about to ask what the borrowing is for.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, used to point out a problem with the last answer

phrases.english: If so, for what

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a challenge to the answer in step 32.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that רב's case is one where the master feeds the slave.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the slave gets food from his master, there seems to be no reason for him to borrow in order to eat.
